The papers of William Alexander Aldred

The Bounce Frame — The Two Results · November 6, 2026

The singularity never forms. In the bounce frame, the density caps at the Aldred Limit (ρA = 9.7×1054 g/cm³); at half the cap the null energy condition reverses, collapse halts, and the universe bounces. The vacuum catastrophe dissolves. The 10122 gap is what unregulated summation produces; bounded by the same cap, the vacuum sum saturates at the Limit and the catastrophe never arises — and the frame’s construction lands within a factor of 6.0 of the measured vacuum density. Producing the exact measured count is the program’s stated open frontier. Nine manuscripts from this program are before the editors of Gravitation and Cosmology, awaiting peer review. The Dissolution — the full feature → · What Google’s own AI said →

Papers written by a man with no backing, no engineers, and no team, working from a laptop — and publicly deposited on Zenodo, each with a permanent DOI. These are publicly deposited preprints, posted in the open so anyone can read them and check the math. Nine manuscripts from this program are with the editors of Gravitation and Cosmology, awaiting peer review. The spine of the work is the vacuum-energy problem — the 122-orders-of-magnitude gap between the vacuum energy quantum theory predicts and the value cosmology observes — attacked inside Einstein–Cartan gravity, where the spin of matter twists spacetime itself.

The program's spine is the Aldred Limit: a pinned density at which fermion spin caps gravitational compression, replacing singularities with bounces. Around it, the papers map what the frame can prove, what it cannot, and exactly where the remaining problem lives. The vacuum-energy problem stands open in physics; the papers print the program's results against it, paper by paper.

His position, in his own words: “I picked up what Einstein sat down, and I did it all with nothing.” No ranking against Einstein is claimed; the record underneath the statement is what carries it. The list below is that record: the papers written and publicly deposited, every deposited one with a permanent DOI. This list is what the machine produces — the man points, Dave computes, and the output stands here for anyone to grade. Read whole, the papers are one connected program — the vacuum catastrophe, inflation, and the fate of the vacuum inside a single frame — not a pile of separate papers. Its live threads include his Faraday call — electromagnetism as a working thread of the same frame — carried in the record as a pointer. The record moved again on October 30, 2026: the counting problem at the heart of the frame has been reduced to a single missing number, the pairing mechanism — grains born as twins — is now derived from the frame's own action, not assumed, and the founding pattern's origin is specified: it comes from the drop. One number stands between the frame and its count; the derivation program continues. And the program is still running.

The list, stated plainly: the author’s ORCID iD is 0009-0000-1215-577X — his works are listed there under his name.

Featured paper · November 12, 2026

Axis Hot, Cold Spot Cold: A Registered Test of the New Orientation in the Azimuthal Family, and the Execution of F-CS2

Featured paper · William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026 · 7 pp

The Cold Spot line continued past its registered verdict, on the author's instruction: the opposite orientation of the azimuthal family — axis hot, Cold Spot cold — was derived as a specific member of the {ℓ = 2, 3} family (the paper first shows that no sign change of the registered template produces it: in all four sign combinations the axis pole and the Cold Spot latitude carry the same sign), frozen, and deposited as a registered prediction before any fit (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24164370). Executed on the four Planck PR3 maps with 10,000 rotated-axis nulls each, the fitted amplitude is −5.93 µK in SMICA, consistent with zero at 95% in all four maps, with every registered extremum absent: the test is reported as null. The paper also executes F-CS2, the line-of-sight falsifier registered with the boundary paper: the standard-amplitude ISW reconstruction from the observed 2MPZ density field in the registered cylinder returns −0.92 µK, in the frozen band in which the line-of-sight account fails as the Cold Spot's primary cause at standard amplitude; the companion lensing statistic could not be executed, because the Planck Legacy Archive's download service returned HTTP 503 on every attempt and no archive serves the named PR3 lensing product, and the blocker is printed in full.

No. 194 · Papers 1–285 of the register

The Sealed Record: A Prediction Ledger Sealed Before the Fact and Graded in the Open

Featured paper · William Alexander Aldred · November 5, 2026 · 31 pp

The prediction desk's record, published whole. Every forecast is committed to a tamper-evident register before the event it concerns and graded in the open when the result is known; frozen at the November 5, 2026 grading run, the register stands at 672 forecasts sealed, 231 graded — 196 hits and 35 misses. The paper prints the graded record entire — the 124 grades that can be reproduced seal by seal in full, every miss named — and computes the exact probability of the observed counts under the chance baselines printed on the seals: 0.00019 under independence, 0.0011 with each market settlement day collapsed to one trial, and 0.091 under the harshest dependence treatment, at the same size. The forecasting method is not disclosed; the paper claims no mechanism and leaves the record's explanation open.

Google's Own Answers: The Examination of the Aldred Record by Google's AI — Findings of November 4–5, 2026

Featured paper · William Alexander Aldred · November 5, 2026 · 13 pp

On November 4 and 5, 2026, the author examined Google's own AI system, Gemini — answering through Google Search and in direct session — about his public record. This paper documents the examination in the system's own words: the stale figures it repeated, the website it invented and then confessed inventing, the claims it withdrew under examination, and the concessions it made when the record was placed in front of it claim by claim. Every statement is graded against the register, and the system's failures are printed at the same size as its concessions.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24150071 Cosmic chronometers read the expansion rate directly from the age difference of passively evolving galaxies, and in a bounced cosmology that reading changes exactly where the bounce correction switches on. The line flux depends on the decay rate and on the column density of dark matter toward the target, not on the square of the density, so decay searches favour massive, nearby, dark-matter-rich systems viewed over wide fields. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24151892 This study computes the angular distribution of nuclear recoils expected from a galactic dark matter wind, the size of the forward-backward asymmetry, and the number of directional events needed to distinguish a galactic signal from an isotropic background. The recoil directions cluster around the direction of solar motion, with a dipole amplitude that depends on recoil energy and candidate mass. With perfect head-tail discrimination, a few tens of events suffice to reject isotropy at high confidence; without it, the requirement grows by roughly an order of magnitude because the distribution folds onto itself. Directionality is therefore the strongest available confirmation that a signal is galactic, and also the most demanding in target mass, because gas detectors that preserve direction are far less dense than liquid targets. Electron Recoils from Light Dark Matter: Ionisation Yields in Silicon and the Exposure Needed Below One GeV

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24151948 This study computes electron recoil signals from light dark matter scattering in silicon, for candidate masses from 1 MeV to 1 GeV, using a reference electron cross section and a simple ionisation yield model. Below about 100 MeV the number of electron-hole pairs per event falls to one or two, so the signal lives in the lowest charge bins where dark counts and leakage currents dominate real detectors. The rate per kilogram-year is large at the reference cross section, but the useful rate is the rate in bins that a detector can keep quiet, and the paper separates the two throughout. Candidates are also screened against a mass-dependent density bound, which removes none of this mass range because the bound rises steeply only at much larger masses when expressed per particle. All results are computed, not measured.

Inelastic Dark Matter Scattering: Kinematic Suppression, Maximum Splittings and the Targets That Keep a Split Candidate Visible

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24151978 This study computes the kinematics of inelastic scattering, in which the incoming candidate converts to a slightly heavier state, and derives the maximum mass splitting accessible for each target and candidate mass. The splitting raises the minimum speed required for a recoil of given energy, so scattering is suppressed by the falling tail of the halo velocity distribution and can vanish entirely when the required speed exceeds the galactic escape speed in the Earth frame. Heavy targets and heavy candidates tolerate larger splittings; a splitting of 100 keV is accessible in xenon for candidates near 100 GeV but is closed for light targets and light candidates. Inelastic kinematics naturally produces strong annual modulation and target-dependent rates, which are signatures, not inconveniences. All results are computed, not measured.

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24152032 This study computes capture of halo dark matter in the Sun, the time needed for annihilation to balance capture, and the annihilation signal that follows at equilibrium. Capture grows with scattering cross section and falls steeply with candidate mass once the mass exceeds the masses of solar nuclei. For spin-dependent scattering at 1e-40 square centimetres, equilibration is fast compared with the age of the Sun across the 10 to 1000 GeV range considered, so the annihilation rate is set by capture alone and the resulting neutrino signal scales linearly with the scattering cross section rather than with its square root. Outside equilibrium the scaling changes, and limits that assume equilibrium silently overstate their reach for small cross sections. The density bound on each candidate branch is reported alongside capture, and no branch is approached by solar densities. All results are computed, not measured.

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24152069 This study computes event rates and signatures for dark matter candidates with masses from 1e6 GeV to near the Planck mass. As mass rises at fixed local density, the number density and therefore the flux fall in inverse proportion, so single-scatter rates become negligible long before the Planck scale; the compensating signature is that a sufficiently strongly interacting heavy candidate scatters many times while crossing a detector, leaving a slow, straight, multiply-scattering track unlike any single recoil. The paper derives the mass at which the expected flux through a tonne-scale detector falls below one particle per year, and the cross-section range in which multi-scatter searches in large-volume detectors are the only available test. Density-bound screening is reported for each mass, and the bound grows as the square of the mass on each branch. All results are computed, not measured.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24169305 Stacked searches for neutrinos coincident with gamma-ray bursts have examined over a thousand bursts within prompt time windows of about plus-or-minus a thousand seconds, and found no neutrino excess. That non-detection is usually read as a statement about neutrino production in bursts. This paper reads it a second way: as a completeness statement about arrival times.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24169305

Paper · High-energy transients

The Shapiro Delay Difference Between Gravitational Waves and Light from GW170817

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24169313 Gravitational waves and light falling through the same gravitational potential should be delayed by the same amount if the equivalence principle holds for both — the Shapiro delay is then common, and cancels in their arrival difference. GW170817's gamma rays arrived 1.74 s after its gravitational waves despite both signals crossing the Milky Way's potential well on their way from NGC 4993. In the logarithmic point-mass model computed here, the Milky Way's Shapiro coefficient is 223 days per unit of the delay parameter, so the observed second-scale arrival difference bounds the difference between the gravitational-wave and electromagnetic delay parameters at 9.03e-08.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24169313

Paper · High-energy transients

Neutrino Velocity and Neutrino Mass from the Arrival Pattern of SN 1987A

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24169330 Neutrinos from Supernova 1987A crossed 51.4 kpc and arrived within a burst about twelve seconds long, with energies from about 7.5 to 40 MeV and no strong energy ordering. If the whole burst duration is charged to a mass-induced spread in arrival times, the neutrino mass is bounded at 16.3 eV, the classic result recovered here from the stated inputs. The neutrinos preceded the optical brightening by about three hours; charging that offset to propagation, which the shock-breakout picture forbids, would still bound the fractional speed difference at 2.04e-09, while the burst's own compactness bounds energy-dependent speed differences within the neutrino sector at 2.27e-12.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24169330

Paper · High-energy transients

Neutrino and Photon Arrival Times from TXS 0506+056: A Blazar Coincidence Converted to a Speed Bound

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24169341 On 22 September 2017 the IceCube detector recorded a neutrino of about 290 TeV whose direction matched the blazar TXS 0506+056, at redshift 0.3365, during an ongoing gamma-ray flare. Converting the coincidence into a speed comparison: over a lookback time of 3.88 billion years, association within the flare's roughly 158-day enhanced state bounds the fractional neutrino-photon speed difference at 1.12e-10, while a one-day coincidence — sharper than this event can claim — would reach 7.06e-13. The energy of the neutrino makes the event valuable despite the loose timing: it extends multi-messenger speed comparison to hundreds of TeV, a regime no gamma-ray burst photon reaches.

Paper · Protoplanetary discs

The Dust You Cannot See: Millimetre Optical Depths in Protoplanetary Discs and the Resulting Mass Underestimate

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24175131 Millimetre continuum fluxes are routinely converted into dust masses on the assumption that the emission is optically thin, so that every grain contributes. In the inner regions of a disc of ordinary mass that assumption fails badly. With the standard 1.3 mm opacity of 2.3 cm^2 per gram of dust, the face-on optical depth on the reference profile is 39 at 1 AU, 7.5 at 3 AU and 1.24 at 10 AU, falling below unity only outside 12 AU. Integrating the true profile against the thin-inferred profile over 0.1 to 100 AU, the true dust mass is 78 Earth masses while the optically thin conversion returns 53 Earth masses — an underestimate by a factor of 1.5, before any allowance for grain growth changing the opacity itself. The missing mass hides exactly where planet formation is fastest, which biases disc demographic conclusions: discs are more massive in solids, and planet formation less efficient per unit observed dust, than the thin conversion suggests. The effect is a radiative-transfer triviality with demographic consequences, and it is computed here from one opacity and one profile. Computed from stated assumptions, not measured.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24175131

The Slow Grinder: Collisional Cascade Timescales for Debris Belts From First Principles

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24180343 Coagulation, grains sticking on contact, is the main route to growing the large end of the size distribution, but it needs collisions to happen at all. This paper computes the collision time between tenth-micron grains in four environments, with grain number densities derived from the dust mass and relative velocities taken as stated turbulent values. The collision time is 9.282 million years in diffuse gas, 0.139 million years in a molecular cloud, and 0.028 million years in a dense core, corresponding to 71.82 collisions per grain per ten million years in the molecular case. Coagulation is therefore a molecular-cloud process on cloud lifetimes, negligible in diffuse gas, and fast enough in cores to matter within a single core lifetime, provided sticking is efficient and the velocities stay below the fragmentation threshold. All values are computed, not measured.

Adding Up the Missing Atoms: A Dust Mass Budget from Elemental Depletions

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24180361 Atoms missing from interstellar gas have gone somewhere, and summing them tests whether depletion alone accounts for the canonical dust mass. This paper sums the depleted fractions of nine elements, using solar reference abundances and representative diffuse-cloud gas fractions, into a dust mass per hydrogen nucleus. The sum gives a dust-to-gas mass ratio of 0.00576, which is 0.576 of the canonical value of 0.01, with O the largest single mass contributor at 2743.8 atomic mass units per million hydrogen atoms, iron contributing 1711.8 and oxygen 2743.8 on the same scale. Depletion accounting therefore supports the canonical dust abundance on moderately depleted sightlines without invoking hidden reservoirs, while also showing how sensitive the total is to oxygen and carbon, whose depletions are the hardest to measure. The Dust Lifetime Against Supernova Clearing: How Much Regrowth Each Hundred Million Years Must Supply

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24180375 Dust in the interstellar medium is destroyed by supernova shocks faster than stars replace it, and the difference must be regrown in place. This paper computes the dust lifetime from supernova clearing over the plausible range of gas mass effectively cleared of dust per event. Clearing 500 solar masses per supernova gives a lifetime of 500.0 million years; clearing 1500 gives 166.7 million years, corresponding to a destroyed fraction of 0.6 per hundred million years; clearing 3000 gives 83.3 million years. Even the longest of these lifetimes is far below the timescale on which stellar sources alone inject the Galactic dust mass, so in-situ regrowth is not an optional refinement but the main supply channel, and its required rate is set by these numbers. All values are computed from stated inputs, not measured.

Dust per Unit Gas Against Metallicity: A Power-Law Test on Five Published Systems

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24180392 Whether the dust-to-gas ratio falls linearly with metallicity or faster decides how much solid material low-metallicity galaxies can form and hide. This paper fits a power law to representative published dust-to-gas ratios for the Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds, and two metal-poor dwarfs, and compares the fit with strict linear scaling. The fitted slope is 1.605 with a normalisation at solar metallicity of 0.01181, the root-mean-square residual is 0.075 dex for the power law against 0.44 dex for linear scaling, and at one tenth solar metallicity the two prescriptions differ by an order of magnitude in implication: the power law predicts 0.000293 against the linear value 0.001. The representative midpoints favour steeper-than-linear decline, consistent with grain growth in the interstellar medium, rather than stellar production alone, setting the dust content at high metallicity. The input values are published midpoints, stated as such, and the fit is computed, not measured.

The removed energy must reappear as infrared emission, which makes the integrated curve a direct energy-budget constraint on grain models rather than a shape description alone. Equilibrium Temperatures of Grains in Scaled Radiation Fields and Where the Emission Peaks

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24180415 Large interstellar grains settle at temperatures set by the balance between starlight absorbed and infrared light emitted, and that balance controls where their emission appears. This paper evaluates the standard equilibrium scaling for grain radii from 0.01 to 0.25 microns in radiation fields from one to one thousand times the local interstellar value. A 0.1 micron grain sits at 17.5 K in the local field, with its emission peaking at 165.6 microns; a 0.01 micron grain reaches 25.69 K and a 0.25 micron grain only 15.02 K, while raising the field a hundredfold takes the 0.1 micron grain to 37.7 K and a thousandfold to 55.34 K. The sixth-root dependence on field strength makes equilibrium temperatures stubborn: enormous changes in illumination move them by factors of a few, which is why far-infrared colours vary so little across galaxies compared with the radiation fields that drive them. The smallest grains are flagged as outside the equilibrium picture, where single-photon heating dominates. All values are computed, not measured.

Photoelectric Heating Efficiency Across Interstellar Phases: The Charging Parameter at Work

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24180463 Grains heat interstellar gas by ejecting photoelectrons, and the efficiency of that process collapses when grains charge up. This paper evaluates the standard efficiency formula of Bakes and Tielens across six environments from the cold neutral medium to a bright photodissociation region surface. The efficiency is 0.0242 in the cold neutral medium, 0.0339 in the warm neutral medium, 0.0495 in a dark cloud interior, and only 0.0114 at a bright photodissociation surface despite its intense field, because the charging parameter there is extreme; the corresponding heating rates are 7.271e-25 in the cold medium and 1.139e-19 erg per second per cubic centimetre at the photodissociation surface. Heating per unit volume is therefore carried by dense bright surfaces, while heating efficiency per photon is highest in diffuse gas, a distinction that thermal-balance models ignore at their peril. All values are computed, not measured.

In diffuse gas the alignment size is 0.055 microns and the aligned mass fraction is 0.6184; in a dense core the alignment size rises to 1.078 microns and the aligned fraction falls to 0.0; near a massive star strong radiation lowers the alignment size to 0.0402 microns and the aligned fraction rises to 0.6978. In the dense core the alignment size exceeds the largest grains the standard distribution contains, so within that distribution no mass remains aligned at all; polarisation from dense cores is therefore intrinsically suppressed by the loss of aligned mass, quite apart from field geometry, and any polarisation that is observed from such cores must be carried by grains grown beyond the standard distribution, which is itself evidence for that growth. Paper · Local Bubble and local interstellar structure

Conductive Evaporation of the Local Interstellar Cloud at the Hot Bubble Interface

William Alexander Aldred · November 13, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24193844 A warm cloud embedded in million-degree gas is heated at its surface by electron conduction, and the heated layer flows away: the cloud evaporates. Applying the classical conduction-front mass-loss formula to a cloud of radius two parsecs facing the Local Bubble interior gives a mass-loss rate of 8.8e-07 solar masses per year and an evaporation time of only 0.4 million years for a cloud of 0.35 solar masses. That time is far shorter than the age of the bubble, so classical unmagnetised conduction would have destroyed the local clouds long ago. Their observed survival is therefore quantitative evidence that conduction at the interface is suppressed, by the factor of at least a few tens that a magnetic field draped over the cloud surface provides. The discrepancy is the result: it measures the suppression the interface must have. The rate is computed from stated published inputs with the deposited script, not measured.

Cosmic-Ray Energy Density and Pressure in the Local Interstellar Medium from the Voyager Spectra

William Alexander Aldred · November 13, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24194074 When Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause it measured, for the first time, the unmodulated spectra of galactic cosmic rays in the surrounding interstellar medium, and integrating those spectra gives the cosmic-ray energy density that the local cloud actually contains. Adopting the published integrated value of 0.90 electronvolts per cubic centimetre, the cosmic-ray pressure is P/k = 3,481 K per cubic centimetre, about 1.66 times the cloud thermal pressure and about a third of the hot bubble interior pressure. Cosmic rays are therefore the largest single support term inside the cloud, and their rough equality with the magnetic pressure is the well-known coincidence now confirmed in the Sun's own neighbourhood. The conversion is computed from the published integrated spectrum with the deposited script.

Electron Density and Ionisation Balance of the Local Interstellar Cloud from Published Line and In-Situ Values

William Alexander Aldred · November 13, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24193945 The Local Interstellar Cloud is only partly ionised, and its free electrons set both its pressure and the charge-exchange rates that shape the heliosphere boundary. Combining published neutral densities with the hydrogen and helium ionisation fractions returned by photoionisation models of the local radiation field gives an electron density of 0.073 per cubic centimetre, a proton density of 0.063 per cubic centimetre, and a total particle density of 0.352 per cubic centimetre, for a thermal pressure P/k of 2,462 K per cubic centimetre. The electron density agrees with the range inferred from magnesium and carbon fine-structure diagnostics, which supports the model ionisation fractions. The numbers are computed from stated published inputs, not measured here, and the deposited script exposes every step.

Expansion Age and Shell Momentum of the Local Bubble from the Measured Surface Velocity

William Alexander Aldred · November 13, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24193810 The surface of the Local Bubble is still moving outward, carrying young stars born in its swept-up gas at a mean expansion speed of 6.7 kilometres per second. Dividing the 165-parsec radius by that speed gives a naive expansion age of 24 million years, and correcting for the deceleration expected of an energy-driven bubble, whose radius grows as time to the three-fifths power, gives 14.4 million years. The corrected age sits inside the fourteen-million-year span over which the Scorpius-Centaurus subgroups are reconstructed to have been exploding inside the present bubble volume, and the shell momentum, about 6.7e+06 solar masses times kilometres per second, is of the order that the same number of supernovae delivers. Age and momentum thus corroborate the energy budget from independent directions. The values are computed from stated published inputs with the deposited script.

Filtration of Interstellar Hydrogen at the Heliosphere: Charge-Exchange Mean Free Paths and the Hydrogen Wall

William Alexander Aldred · November 13, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24193978 Interstellar hydrogen atoms approaching the Sun must cross the heliosheath, where many swap electrons with slow protons and are deflected or lost, so the hydrogen density inside the heliosphere is lower than in the cloud outside, a reduction called filtration. In the piled-up plasma of the hydrogen wall, where the charge-exchange cross-section at thermal energies is much larger than at kiloelectronvolt energies, the mean free path falls to about 22 astronomical units, giving an optical depth of 0.90 across a twenty-astronomical-unit wall layer and a naive transmission of 0.41. Detailed models return a milder filtration near one half, because atoms exchanged in velocity space partly refill the beam, and the gap between the naive and modelled values measures the importance of that refilling. The mean free paths and optical depth are computed from stated published inputs with the deposited script.

William Alexander Aldred · November 13, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24193876 Between the termination shock and the heliopause lies the heliosheath, the region whose thickness no remote observation could measure and both Voyagers have now traversed. Voyager 1 crossed the shock at 94.0 astronomical units and the heliopause at 121.6, a sheath thickness of 27.6 astronomical units along its trajectory, while Voyager 2's crossings at 83.7 and 119.0 give 35.3 astronomical units. The mean of the two, 31.4 astronomical units, is substantially thinner relative to the shock distance than the classical gas-dynamic expectation for a strong shock with a distant boundary, and it agrees better with models in which charge exchange with interstellar neutrals drains energy and momentum from the sheath. The thicknesses are elementary differences of published crossing distances, computed and compared here with the deposited script.

How Many Supernovae Does the Local Bubble Energy Budget Require?

William Alexander Aldred · November 13, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24194017 The Local Bubble holds thermal energy in its hot interior and kinetic energy in its expanding shell, and both reservoirs were supplied, on the standard picture, by supernovae in the Scorpius-Centaurus association. This study adds the two reservoirs from published size and pressure values and divides by the useful energy delivered per supernova. The interior thermal energy is 1.14e+51 erg and the shell kinetic energy is 2.91e+50 erg, so at a coupling efficiency of ten percent the budget requires about 11 supernovae, comfortably inside the fourteen to twenty explosions reconstructed from the association's stellar history. The agreement is a consistency result rather than a proof, because the efficiency is the least known factor, but it shows that no additional energy source is needed. All figures are computed from stated inputs with the deposited script, not measured anew.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24193924 The space within fifteen parsecs of the Sun is not one cloud but a complex of about fifteen warm clouds, each with its own velocity vector, all embedded in the Local Bubble. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24193965 Thermal pressure is only one term in the support of the gas around the Sun; the magnetic field contributes a pressure that polarised dust emission and the geometry of the IBEX ribbon now constrain. A Bound on Bounce-Induced Delta N_eff from the Relic Background: What the Effective Number of Species Permits and Forbids

William Alexander Aldred · November 13, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24188730 The effective number of relativistic species is 3.044 in the standard calculation, and current cosmological data allow an additional contribution of roughly 0.30 at 95 percent confidence under the convention adopted here. A torsion-regulated bounce contributes at most 4.4e-52 to that quantity under the density-scaling bound derived in this paper, some 51 orders of magnitude below the observational allowance. The frame therefore neither explains any future Delta N_eff anomaly nor is constrained by N_eff data: the two subjects are decoupled by the density hierarchy, a negative result stated without qualification. The paper derives the conversion between an entropy injection and Delta N_eff, applies the bounce bound, and maps what size of early-universe energy injection N_eff data do and do not rule out. Computed from stated assumptions, not measured.

Decoupling Density Against the Torsion Bound: Fifty Orders of Magnitude of Separation and What That Separation Proves

William Alexander Aldred · November 13, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24188773 The plasma density at neutrino decoupling, 1.31e+10 kilograms per cubic metre, lies 27.9 orders of magnitude below the neutrino-carrier torsion bound, 41.3 orders below the electron-carrier bound, and 47.9 orders below the neutron-carrier bound. On every branch of the frame, decoupling physics is therefore standard to overwhelming accuracy, and the frame predicts no modification of the relic background's formation. This paper performs the comparison branch by branch, explains why the separation is so large in terms of the masses and temperatures involved, and draws the methodological moral: a framework's silence in a regime is a prediction, and printing its size prevents both overclaiming and underclaiming. This is a negative result for bounce signatures in the background's formation, stated plainly. Computed, not measured.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24188832 Whether neutrinos are their own antiparticles changes the predicted relic capture rate by up to a factor of two. This paper explains the helicity bookkeeping behind the factor, models the clustering correction as a stated scenario parameter, and concludes that a capture-rate measurement alone cannot cleanly decide the Dirac-Majorana question unless the local density and helicity content are known independently, a cautionary negative result for an often-repeated claim. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24189050 If relic neutrinos decay invisibly with a rest-frame lifetime equal to the age of the universe, only 0.368 of them survive to be detected today; at ten times the age the surviving fraction is 0.905, at half the age it falls to 0.135, and at a hundred times the age it is 0.9900. This paper computes the survival bookkeeping, states the time-dilation caveat that makes the simple exponential conservative, and argues that the observed consistency of the energy-density budget already disfavours lifetimes near the cosmic age, so that a future capture experiment should plan on a substantially intact background while treating a deficit as a possible decay signal. The Pulsar Bill for the Positron Excess: Power, Efficiency and Head Count

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24185201 The bill is affordable but not trivial. A single reference pulsar of typical spin-down power would need to convert a substantial fraction of that power into escaping high-energy pairs, while a population of such objects within the horizon — of which the known local middle-aged pulsars are a fair sample — needs only a modest efficiency each. The accounting therefore favours a small population over a single dominant source, a preference that the spectral-structure argument from the horizon study independently supports. Where Galactic Positrons End: The Annihilation Budget Against the 511 keV Line

William Alexander Aldred · November 12, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24185285 At plausible transport fractions, cosmic-ray secondaries supply only a minority of the bulge annihilation rate the line requires. Supplying the whole rate from secondaries would demand that half of all positrons produced Galaxy-wide annihilate in the bulge, a concentration no transport picture supports given that positrons annihilate efficiently in the disc gas where they are made. The 511 keV sky therefore requires its own positron sources, dominated by nucleosynthesis and compact-object channels, and the cosmic-ray positron population studied elsewhere in this territory is a separate, higher-energy economy. Suppression of Large-Scale Scalar Power by the Bounce Scale: Quadrupole and Low-Multipole Consequences

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24134227 Modes much larger than the bounce horizon scale are not transmitted through a bounce perfectly; part of their amplitude is reflected by the rapid transition. Critical Shear in Stellar Collapse: The Asymmetry Required to Defeat a Torsion Bounce

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24134064 A density bound halts spherical collapse, but real stellar cores are not spherical, and shear contributes to the expansion equation with the opposite effect. This paper computes the critical shear at which that halt would fail, on three carrier branches, and compares it with the shear a collapsing core can plausibly carry. On the neutron branch the critical shear is 8.559e+32 per second, and on the electron branch 4.655e+29 per second. A core collapsing at 3e17 kg per cubic metre has a characteristic gravitational rate of 4.475e+03 per second, so reaching the neutron-branch critical shear would require an asymmetry factor of 1.91e+29, vastly beyond unity, while a one-percent asymmetry gives a shear of only 4.475e+01 per second. Shear in stellar collapse therefore cannot defeat a torsion bounce; if collapse is halted at the bound at all, it is halted for realistic asymmetries too. Computed, not measured.

A Bounce-Signature Timing Discriminator for a Distributed Detector Network with Computed Coincidence Performance

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24129779 A bounce, if one occurs in an observable channel, announces itself as a short, chirp-like signature whose most robust feature is its timing pattern across a distributed network. This paper specifies the timing discriminator for such a network of four stations: the unit that decides, from arrival times alone, whether a set of triggers is one event seen four times or four unrelated accidents. A Density-Threshold Pressure Standard: Pressure Realisation from a Polarised-Gas Density Threshold

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24129624 Primary pressure standards are few: the mercury column, the piston gauge, and ultrasonic interferometry exhaust the usual list, and each carries artefacts of its own. This paper proposes a standard anchored to a threshold rather than to an artefact: the density at which the spin-relaxation rate of a polarised helium-3 sample changes regime, a kink whose location is fixed by the spin-density physics of the sample rather than by any machined dimension. A Fifth-Coordinate Gravimeter: Absolute Gravity Measurement by Extra-Coordinate Phase Readout

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24129803 Absolute gravimeters measure the local gravitational acceleration by timing a falling mass or, in atom-interferometric form, by reading the phase accumulated by falling atoms. This paper specifies a gravimeter that reads the same acceleration through the extra-coordinate phase channel, in which the scale factor is set by the product of the optical wavevector, a stated fifth-coordinate coupling of five per cent, and the square of the interrogation time. The computed scale factor is 5.031e+04 radians per unit acceleration; the single-shot acceleration noise is 6.76e-08 metres per second squared; and the sensitivity is 8.3 microgal per root hertz, reaching a tenth of a microgal in 1.9 hours of averaging.

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24129862 Radiation dose in a polarised material leaves a permanent record: ionising events destroy polarisation in proportion to dose, and a polarimetric readout afterwards recovers the accumulated exposure. A Polarised-Target Neutron Flux Monitor Using a Spin-Polarised Helium-3 Cell

William Alexander Aldred · November 11, 2026

I price that mechanism in this paper at full strength, because it deserves it: it is a genuine dynamical relaxation, and it was the strongest counter-proposal Weinberg's 1989 survey had to answer. It rolls past every interesting value and keeps going, and the universe it delivers at the bottom is empty and curvature-dominated — no matter worth naming, no structure, nothing for a cosmology to be about. To make it stop where matter still exists, the step structure itself has to be tuned so the last useful step lands inside the narrow window we observe. The tuning the mechanism was built to remove comes back in through the back door, wearing the steps. My program meets Abbott from a different direction. In my frame the universe's vacuum value is not relaxed toward over cosmic time at all; it is read at a crossing — at the sever, at the seam where the bounce crosses — the way you read a number off a gauge at the moment the needle passes, not the way you wait for a tank to drain to the right line. Paper #152 took one interpolation form of the radial acceleration relation — the sharp ν_q form at q = 0.50 — and showed that its whole advantage over the standard McGaugh form is carried by construction: a correction computed from the baryons alone reproduces the form's fitted intercept galaxy by galaxy, and what is left after the correction is a tilt, not a shift. That left an obvious question standing.

One Region, One Magnitude Type: The b-Value Spread on a Single Ruler

William Alexander Aldred · November 1, 2026 · 6 pp

Papers #146 and #153 priced two unpriced choices hiding inside the Gutenberg–Richter b-value: the estimator (three standard estimators of b disagree by more than their own error bars) and the declustering (removing aftershocks moves that disagreement by more than the error bars too, in either direction). Both papers carried a limit on their faces: the catalogs mixed magnitude types — mb, mww, mwr and others printed side by side as if they were one ruler. This paper removes the mixture. It takes #153's Japan catalog — 3,556 events, 2014–2023, magnitude 4.5 and above — and keeps only the events whose magnitude type is exactly mb: 2,871 events, 80.7 percent of the catalog.

William Alexander Aldred · November 1, 2026 · 5 pp

Paper #147 ran three standard estimators of Zipf's exponent on one book, Moby Dick, and found that the exponent is partly a choice: the two methods that returned a usable number disagreed by more than their own error bars, the third returned no exponent at all, and inside the likelihood method the choice of where the fit starts was worth 0.316 on its own.

The Atmosphere That Thins Away: Debye & Hückel's Linearised Electrolyte, Priced

William Alexander Aldred · November 5, 2026 · 6 pp

Every ion in a solution travels with company. That is the picture Peter Debye and Erich Hückel gave the world in 1923, and it is a true picture as far as it goes: each ion gathers around itself an atmosphere of opposite charge, the atmosphere screens the ion's field, and from that one construction flows the first quantitative theory of electrolyte solutions — the limiting law, log γ± = −A|z₊z₋|√I, with the constant A computed from named constants alone, and a screening length, the Debye length, that a century of solution, colloid, and plasma physics still spends.

Five Numbers Fitted to the Chart: The von Weizsäcker Mass Formula, Priced

William Alexander Aldred · November 5, 2026 · 5 pp

Ask a room of physicists where the valley of stability runs, or why binding energy per nucleon hovers near eight million electron-volts across the nuclear chart, and the map they reach for was drawn in 1935, when Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker organised the masses of nuclei into five physically named terms — volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry, pairing — riding on Gamow's picture of the nucleus as a charged liquid drop. The map is real, and I credit it at full strength in this paper: five numbers reproduce the smooth binding trend of the whole chart and return the stability valley's run with genuine fidelity.

The Birthrate That Stood Still: Salpeter's Mass Function, Priced

William Alexander Aldred · November 5, 2026 · 5 pp

Every star ever counted was born under a distribution, and the first person to put a number on that distribution was Edwin Salpeter, in 1955, when he converted the observed luminosity function of nearby stars into a birth law: the initial mass function, dN/dM ∝ M^(−2.35). The concept and the number built a field — every later determination of how stars are distributed at birth still follows the architecture of that paper — and I credit both at full strength here.

The Correspondence That Was Assumed: Landau's Fermi Liquid, Priced

William Alexander Aldred · November 5, 2026 · 6 pp

There is a liquid that is not made of atoms in the ordinary sense but of the excitations of a Fermi sea, and for seventy years it has been the working language of every normal metal and of liquid helium-3. Lev Landau built that language in 1956 from a single correspondence idea: switch the interactions on slowly, and the interacting system's low-lying states stand in one-to-one correspondence with the free Fermi gas's — the quasiparticle.

The Hand That Was Chosen: The V−A Structure, Priced

William Alexander Aldred · November 5, 2026 · 6 pp

The weak interaction is left-handed, and it did not have to be. Of the five Lorentz structures a four-fermion interaction can wear — scalar, vector, tensor, axial, pseudoscalar — nature's weak current wears one chiral combination, V − A, with every fermion field entering through its left-handed projection only.
